pr_title: Don't allow null converters and add Path support to NotSupportedException
pr_body:
Address feedback and issues from https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/2259 including
- Nulls were being passed to converters when using collections. Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/32523
- Per discussion, we should not support `JsonConverterFactory.CreateConverter()` returning _null_
- Extra boxing avoided. Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/32147

Note after this PR is in, there will be a follow-up PR that adds the correct XML doc regarding exceptions.

### Details on JsonConverterFactory.CreateConverter()` should not return _null._
After this PR we align with 3.0\3.1 behavior of not supporting _null._

When a _null_ value was returned from `CreateConverter()` the previous code (and in 3.0\3.1) threw `ArgumentNullException`. This was changed to `InvalidOperationException` and an exception message was added.

Background: allowing null from `CreateConverter()` was done in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/2259 because before that PR the collection code threw a "nice" exception that contained the parent Type and property name. Before that PR, this could not be done in `CreateConverter()` because collections were not converters and didn't share that code path. With https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/2259 collections became converters, and thus needed a way to identify a "not supported" case so code further up the call stack could throw the "nice" exception message. If a `NotSupportedException` was thrown directly from within `CreateConverter()` then the message would only contain the name of the Type that is not supported, not the parent Type or the property name.

Per offline discussion, it was decided we would add Path information to `NotSupportedException` similarly like we do for `JsonException`. This means throwing a `NotSupportedException` directly from a converter (or converter factory) would re-throw the exception with Path appended to the original message.

Examples of the previous exceptions:
```The type 'System.Int32[,]' on 'System.Text.Json.Serialization.Tests.ExceptionTests+ClassWithInvalidArray.UnsupportedArray' is not supported.```
or if a converter threw its own `NotSupportedException` or the exception occurred in a collection element Type, not the property Type:
```The type 'System.Int32[,]' is not supported.```

The latter case is especially bad because it provided no way to determine where the unsupported Type exists in the JSON or the object graph.

Examples of exceptions with this PR:
``` The type 'System.Int32[,]' is not supported. The unsupported member type is located on type 'System.Text.Json.Serialization.Tests.GenericIEnumerableWrapper`1[System.Int32[]]'. Path: $.UnsupportedDictionary."```
or this (for read cases):
``` The type 'System.Int32[,]' is not supported. The unsupported member type is located on type 'System.Text.Json.Serialization.Tests.GenericIEnumerableWrapper`1[System.Int32[]]'. Path: $.UnsupportedDictionary | LineNumber: 0 | BytePositionInLine: 10."```

### Details on extra boxing avoided
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/2259 added an extra box+unbox for value types passed into the root. This PR fixes that. In addition, for structs that have their own converter (and thus are not treated as "POCO structs" with properties) no boxing occurs at all (previously and in 3.0\3.1 a box was done).

In addition, boxing operations were removed that helped reduce non-stack boxing. The result is less stack allocations and boxing\unboxing. There doesn't appear to be any significant CPU performance changes but there is some minor reductions in allocations:

pr_comments:
Unrelated and previously hit CI failures in:
System.Diagnostics.PerformanceCounter.Tests
System.Net.Http.Functional.Tests.HttpClientTest
This PR introduced a breaking change - https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/35422. See that issue for more info. I'll file a breaking change doc.

Update: a breaking change doc was already filed: https://github.com/dotnet/docs/issues/20823, https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/compatibility/3.1-5.0#jsonserializerserialize-throws-argumentnullexception-when-type-parameter-is-null.

https://github.com/dotnet/docs/issues/20823 was meant to cover https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/528#issuecomment-589298591 not this, but if they surface in the same API / behavior then agree we don't need two.
@ericstj on a second look, the breaking change was made in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/528 but refactored in this PR. So this PR wasn't the breaking change.

issue_context.title: When serializing arrays and dictionaries, null values are being passed to the custom JsonConverter<T>.Write method
comments:
Re-opening. Please clean up the TODO comments in source that link to this issue and update nullability (these comments were introduced in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/32474).

For example:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/385b4d4296f9c5cb82363565aa210a1a37f92d90/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/JsonConverterOfT.cs#L70-L75

I am going to assume all the test cases/examples are now covered :)

review_comments:
This case does not include the Path because this throws on `Initialize` and we can only append Path information once we get into the ReadCore loop, right? 

Did you consider wrapping `state.Initialize` on a try-catch block so we can append the Path on this case?

Yes per discussion the root type would always have "$" as the path and also the Type information would just be the `<T>` passed in (or `returnType` argument) so it is not normally useful.

Adding the extra `try\catch` is possible but does add a little cost in terms of performance and makes the code a bit more difficult to follow since now we have just a single `try\catch` and wrapping it would cause at least 3 more.

Can we keep consistency and either just return the `T` value or make this a void method and set the return value in `state.Current.ReturnValue`? Why does the returning value needs to be different to state's `ReturnValue`?

Without the check, we'll get a NullReferenceException.

If we use `state.Current.ReturnValue` then we will box (again).
Let's add a test for this branch.
